b: It’s never been easier to find great recipes to experiment with in the kitchen. You can pull them from viral TikToks, up-and-coming Substackers who are reviving the idea of an old-school food blog, or the classic archives of chefs like Alton Brown. What’s harder to come by are some of the basic skills needed to actually make those recipes — and have them turn out well. Cooking can be a manly art, but like all arts, it requires learning and mastering a discrete set of techniques. Once you get them down, they become second nature, but they sure don’t start out that way.

I remember fumbling around our small apartment kitchen in my early 20s, trying to take some of the cooking load off my wife. I didn’t have much of a culinary education (a child of the ‘90s, I grew up on boxed dinners and canned veggies), so I made plenty of clunky errors that could have been avoided had I sought out and practiced a few fundamentals.

What follows are the kitchen skills that every man should have in his toolkit. These aren’t full how-tos; for that, YouTube is a goldmine, since it really helps to visually see what’s happening on a counter or stovetop. Think of this as more of a checklist for your culinary self-education — a road map to what it takes to know your way around a kitchen.
1. How to Read and Follow a Recipe

Following a recipe seems like a pretty straightforward task — until you get halfway through and realize you’ve mucked things up and it’s already taken twice as long as the recipe said. Before you start cooking, read through the entire recipe and make sure it all makes sense to you: that you have the ingredients, that you know how each needs to be prepped, and that you understand the sequence and flow of the steps. The reality is that following a recipe sometimes requires more practical wisdom than you’d think, especially the first time through.
2. How to Cut Vegetables and Herbs

After you’ve properly read a recipe, it’s time to prep your ingredients. You’ll often find adjectives next to vegetables or other ingredients like “sliced,” “chopped,” “minced,” etc. Knowing what those terms mean and how to execute them — how to use a knife to chop an onion, slice an avocado, mince garlic, and so on — is not as obvious as it might seem. And for some things, there are tips and tricks that’ll make the task easier. Watch some YouTube tutorials for each specific skill, or click here for a couple of AoM photo tutorials.

I have a good friend who used to host an annual chili night in the fall. The first year she made chili, she put in a tablespoon of cayenne powder rather than a teaspoon. That first taste served as a good reminder of how important proper measurements are. Especially for spices. Knowing how to measure dry vs. wet ingredients as well as how those measurements are abbreviated — e.g., a lowercase ‘t’ (tsp) is a teaspoon; a capital ‘T’ (Tbsp) is a tablespoon — is truly a foundational kitchen skill.
4. How to Heat (and Grease) a Pan

Before you turn a stovetop burner on, you need to know if you should use high, medium, or low heat (medium-high is generally a safe bet and the temperature setting you’ll use most). Then, before you put food in the pan, you’ll want to preheat it for at least a few minutes, often greased with some sort of fat (butter, oil, cooking spray), which prevents food from sticking, ensures even heating, and promotes the all-important Maillard reaction.

The temperature to which you initially heat the pan may not be the one you use throughout the cooking process. Sometimes you’ll start something high, but then move to lower heat (or occasionally the reverse). Think searing a steak on high and then turning it down to finish cooking, or bringing a soup to a boil before dropping it to a simmer.

The stovetop skills keep coming — and we aren’t done yet. If you haven’t already, you’ll quickly realize that the stovetop is really the epicenter of the home kitchen. To sauté something is simply to cook it in a hot pan with oil, butter, or another fat. Nearly anything can be sautéed, but it’s usually meats and/or vegetables, cut into smallish, uniform pieces.

Besides sautéing, perhaps the next most common cooking method for meats and vegetables of all kinds is roasting, which practically means cooking it in the oven. (Technically, roasting is cooking with hot air that evenly surrounds the food, which is why you want to give things some room on the pan, so they brown instead of steam.) It’s a more hands-off method of cooking and can be utilized for even large chunks of meat like whole birds, shoulders, ribs, etc.

Simmering is most similar to boiling as a cooking method, but a simmer is kept at a temperature just below boiling. It tenderizes food, blends flavors together, and thickens sauces through gentle evaporation. Simmering tends to require a little more attention — keeping the temperature just right may require regular adjustments — but can be used for a number of different foods, be it soup in a large pot or sliced veggies in a shallow pan.

Did you know you can cook pasta the wrong way? Take it from Brett: “I didn’t realize I was making it wrong until after I got married; Kate was aghast to see me put the pasta in right after filling up the pot with water, instead of waiting for the water to boil. A recipe for mushy pasta.”
Boil the water first, add a generous amount of salt, then add the pasta and be sure to stir so it doesn’t stick.

Ground meat isn’t necessarily a sexy star in the food world, but it’s surprisingly versatile: tacos, casseroles, soups, etc. It just needs to be cooked first. Similar to pasta, you don’t want to throw cold meat on a cold pan. Preheat the pan, break up the meat into small bits with a spatula, and cook until the pink spots are gone. It’s a little harder to tell when white meats or sausage are fully cooked, but you’ll get the hang of it with practice.

I’ve heard professional chefs say that the difference between their meals and yours basically comes down to seasoning. Home chefs are generally pretty timid with their seasonings, salt in particular, and it can lead to bland-tasting food even when everything else is done right. Learn to be liberal with seasonings — even going beyond what a recipe calls for — by tasting as you go and adding a bit more at a time.
12. How to Make and Use a Marinade

A marinade is a sauce that you soak a raw food in. That’s it. It’s usually cuts of chicken, pork, or steak that are marinated, but seafood and veggies are common too. I used to think the purpose of a marinade was to saturate an entire cut of meat, but it’s actually mostly about coating the outside of the food to give it a flavor-packed, caramelized exterior when it cooks. The liquid will certainly penetrate some, but not all the way. For more tips and recipes, check out our guide to marinades.

I fancy myself to be pretty good in the kitchen, but thawing meat is one of the things that still regularly gets my goat. It’s a tricky and inconsistent science. When possible, meat should be fully thawed to refrigerator temperature before cooking (unless you’re using a crockpot/Instant Pot). Having frozen spots will lengthen the cooking process as well as provide inconsistent temperatures across the cut — you don’t want the ends of a tenderloin fully cooked while the middle is icy. There are shortcuts for when you’re in a pinch, but the safest way is to think ahead and put frozen meat in the fridge a few days before you’re planning on cooking it.
14. How to Use a Meat Thermometer

Chicken breast is often cited as being among the most intimidating pieces of meat to cook. That anxiety can be totally alleviated by simply using a meat thermometer while cooking — and it applies to other meats as well. Knowing what the internal temperature should be for chicken (165°), pork (145°-155°), and beef (135°-150°) will come in tremendously handy as a home chef. (Temperatures vary for different cuts of meat; do your homework.)
Bonus: a thermometer can also be used for baked goods, casseroles, and even homemade yogurt.

Cracking an egg is one of those skills that requires little more than practice, practice, practice. Egg-cracking 201, which should also be in your repertoire, includes cracking an egg with one hand as well as separating the yolk from the white (a somewhat common requirement in baked goods).

KitchenAid stand mixers look pretty sharp on a countertop — like you know what you’re doing around the kitchen. They also have a reputation in too many households for being mere decoration rather than actually being used. Knowing how to use a mixer for bread doughs, dessert batters, and homemade whipped cream (and which attachment — hook, paddle, or whisk — is used for each) will take your kitchen game up a notch. Handheld mixers are also nice to know how to use.

Few kitchen skills are as satisfying as successfully carving a Thanksgiving turkey in front of your friends and family. Confidently slicing up a roasted bird with a sharp knife and a large platter at hand has a way of making you feel you’ve earned your place at the head of the table. This skill can be applied to any cooked bird, and once you get the hang of it, it’s like riding a bike.
